passages.where: Listen to counsel, the proverb says, for many plans are in a person's heart but the purpose of the LORD will prevail. The site's note says the one Hebrew word etsah covers both the counsel a young person should listen to and the purpose of the LORD that stands, and the chapter asks the reader to take both seriously. A plan for new work is weighed against the counsel of others and laid before God's purpose.

A man's heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps. The site's note says the chapter opens with the densest group of sayings about the LORD in the collection: people make plans and weigh their own motives, but the LORD weighs hearts, establishes steps and decides outcomes. Planning is not forbidden here; it is placed under someone.

God tells Abram to leave his country, his kindred and his father's household for a land he will be shown. The site's note says the command names no destination and asks Abram to act on God's word alone, and that Abram went at seventy-five. A late start is not counted against him anywhere in the story.

Ordered home by the priest of Bethel, Amos answers that he was no prophet but a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-figs when the LORD took him from following the flock. The site's note on the chapter says he answers that he was a herdsman whom the LORD called. His authority did not come from the right training or the right family.

Jesus calls two fishermen at work, promising to make them fishers of men, and they leave their nets at once. The site's plain note says Jesus did not ask them to stop being who they were: fishermen would still be fishers, now of people. It asks which skills and habits of ordinary work Jesus could use, and which nets he may be asking you to leave.

Sent to Pharaoh at the burning bush, Moses asks who he is to go, and God answers that he will surely be with him. The site's note says God does not answer Moses' sense of inadequacy by building up his confidence but by promising his own presence, a pattern that returns with Gideon and Jeremiah. The note on the chapter says he was tending his father-in-law's flock when the call came.

Serving wine to the Persian king, Nehemiah is asked what he wants, prays silently to the God of heaven, and asks to be sent to rebuild the city of his fathers. The site's note on the chapter says the king grants him leave, letters and materials. A settled post at court was left for harder work, with a prayer between the question and the answer.

After two roads were closed to them, Paul sees a man of Macedonia pleading for help, and the group concludes that God has called them there. The site's plain note says Paul's plans were blocked twice before the right road opened and he did not know why at the time. It notices how they decided: not on a feeling alone, but by talking together about what God seemed to be showing them.

James rebukes those who plan their business as if tomorrow were theirs to command, and tells them to say instead, if the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that. The site's plain note asks whether God is anywhere in your plans for this year. James does not tell anyone to stop planning; he tells them to plan as people whose life is a mist.

After the resurrection Peter announces that he is going fishing, the others go with him, and they catch nothing all night. The site's plain note says Peter went back to what he knew after a failure, and Jesus met him there, in his ordinary work, and fed him. Going back to old work is not where God stops looking for a person.

misread.taken: Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was called is quoted as if it forbade a Christian to change jobs, so that wanting different work were itself a lack of contentment.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Paul tells believers they do not have to change their station to be acceptable to God, and then asks the other side: where do you have the freedom to change something, and are you taking it. In the next verse the BSB reads that a slave who can gain freedom should take the opportunity; the note sets out a second reading of that verse, held by other translations, and does not choose between them. On either reading the passage is about a person's worth before God not depending on their station, and not a rule against new work.

whole: People come to this question from very different places. Some are restless and cannot say why. Some have been unhappy in their work for years and are only now admitting it. Some have a skill or a longing that their job never used. Some are being pushed by a change in the industry, a health problem or a family need. And some are being pulled by something they can hardly name, a sense that God may be asking for something else. Many feel two pressures at once: the bills, the years already invested and the people who depend on them on one side, and on the other the fear of wasting the one life they have.

Scripture does not treat a change of work as suspicious or as automatically holy. Abram left his country at seventy-five. Amos was a herdsman when the LORD took him from the flock. Moses was tending another man's sheep, Nehemiah was a royal servant, and the fishermen left their nets. Peter also went back to fishing after his worst failure, and Jesus met him there. The difficulty is that the heart is not a good judge of its own restlessness. James warns against planning as if tomorrow were ours, and Proverbs says that many plans are in a person's heart while the LORD's purpose prevails. The same restlessness can be a call or a way of running from a hard place, and from the inside the two can feel the same.

So the Bible's wisdom asks for patience and company. Listen to counsel, as the proverb says, and let people who know you and your obligations speak into it. Pray before you answer, as Nehemiah did in the space of a breath and as the psalm asks to be taught. Weigh your gifts, your duties to the people who depend on you and the real needs your work could meet, not only the salary or the status. Notice closed doors without despairing at them; Paul's plans were blocked twice before Macedonia, and his group decided by talking it through together. Plan, and hold the plan as one who says if the Lord is willing. Where money or a contract is at stake, get proper advice before you jump.

The hope Scripture gives is that the one who calls goes with those he sends. Moses asked who he was, and God answered that he would be with him. Jesus did not ask the fishermen to stop being fishermen, and he met Peter at the boat after everything had gone wrong. Whether you stay or go, the work is done before God, and nothing you have learned is wasted in his hands.
sit: Are you running toward something or away from something, and who could help you tell the difference?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note calls Psalm 143 a prayer that asks to be taught, and says to pick one of its short prayers and pray it: let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, or teach me to do Your will.
